question: The pandemic highlighted the importance of online education. Nonetheless, significant challenges remain, such as inequalities in access to digital infrastructure, the need for quality digital educational content and training teachers in new technologies. In view of the Digital Education Action Plan 2021-2027: 1.
How does the Commission assess progress in the implementation of the EU’s online education strategies and what key challenges have been identified?
Are there any initiatives aiming to close the digital divide between Member States, so that all pupils and students have equal access to online education?
How does it plan to support teacher training in modern digital skills and teaching methods using technology?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.3.2025) The Digital Education Action Plan1 (DEAP) sets out a vision for high-quality and inclusive digital education. Its implementation started in 2021 and is fully on track. The Commission is currently undertaking the DEAP’s review, which will demonstrate progress to date and highlight persisting and emerging challenges.

The findings will be published alongside the Roadmap on the future of digital education and training2, contributing to the objectives of the Union of Skills. The Roadmap will pave the way for the Commission’s future initiatives to support digital education in Europe.

Under the current Plan, the Council Recommendation on the key enabling factors for successful digital education and training3, adopted in 2023, promotes equitable and impactfocused investment in digital education: Member States are called to provide equal access to all learners by investing in high-speed internet connectivity in all education and training institutions and close territorial and socio-economic gaps, in line with the EU-level targets for the Digital Decade Programme 20304.

The online tool SELFIE (Self-reflection on Effective Learning by Fostering the use of Innovative Educational technologies) for Teachers5 supports the digital skills of educators, complemented by the work done through the Teachers’ Academies6, which support educators’ professional development, including on digital skills.

Substantial EU funds are devoted to digital education and skills: the Recovery and Resilience Facility7 (EUR 25.7 billion), Cohesion Policy funds8 (the European Social Fund Plus and the European Regional Development Fund) and the Erasmus+ programme (EUR 834.2 million in 2023)9.
